flocks:item-handbooktext-flocks:creature: Greylag geese come north in spring and spend the summer on lakes, then fly south again in autumn. A flock floats together near the shore and paddles away from anyone who comes near. Get too close, or let a shot fly past, and the whole flock takes off and comes down elsewhere on the lake, or on another lake. They remember it: see Birds.

Mallards live on lakes and ponds from early spring to late autumn, in smaller groups than geese, on smaller water. They let you a little closer than geese do, spring almost straight up off the water when alarmed and fly fast and low. Drakes have a green head and a white collar; hens are mottled brown. Golden eagles hunt them.

Grey herons stand alone, or in pairs, in still water one block deep. They wait hunched for a long time, stalk slowly through the shallows and strike at fish. A heron is wary: it backs away and then takes off from further off than ducks, and flies with slow, deep wingbeats to other shallows.

Golden eagles live all year over open high ground. An eagle perches on a peak, a crag or a tall tree, soars in circles on rising air, and when it sees a hare or a mallard in the open below, it stoops on it at great speed. A pond an eagle keeps hunting soon empties of ducks. Perched or feeding, it takes off when someone comes near; in the air it pays them no heed.

Carrion crows live all year on open land with trees about: meadows, forest edges and farmland. A small group walks about pecking at the ground. Crows are wary: they walk off when someone comes near and, if they come closer, fly up into the nearest trees, cawing, and wait there until the coast is clear. At dusk they go up into the trees to roost. They eat crops, as hares do, and fly over fences; a straw dummy keeps them off.

Herring gulls live on the sea along the coast all year round, in loose groups. They are bold, letting people come much closer than other waterbirds, and noisy, with a laughing call. Every so often a group goes up of its own accord, wheels over the water for a while and settles again further along the shore. Gulls get used to people: it takes a lot more to drive them off a stretch of coast than it does geese.

Tawny owls live all year in woods and among the trees around farmland, each alone in its own patch. By day an owl roosts on a branch deep in a tree's crown, close to the trunk and hidden in the leaves, and sits tight: it only flies when someone is nearly under it, and then to another tree. At dusk it moves out into the open, onto a tree top at the edge of the woods, a fence post or a wall, and watches the ground; when a wood mouse comes out it glides down onto it without a sound and swallows it. Through the night you hear it: a long hoot, a pause, then a quavering one, and now and then a sharp "ke-wick". At dawn it goes back to roost.

Wood mice live in the grass of meadows, forest edges and open woods. They are few, and seldom seen: by day they sleep curled up in the grass, and they come out at night to nibble and sniff about, running from anyone who comes near. They are what tawny owls hunt.
game:item-handbooktext-strawdummy:
A Straw dummy standing in the ground can be picked up using shift + rightmouse click

It is also a scarecrow that never stops working: crows won't raid crops or come down to feed within 15 blocks of a standing straw dummy, and crows already there fly off. See Birds.
gamemechanicinfo-birds-text:
Birds
Signs of the seasons.

Migration
In spring and autumn, flocks of greylag geese and common cranes pass high overhead in long V's, calling: toward the pole in spring, toward the equator in autumn. Near the equator, where they spend the winter, they don't migrate. In spring some of the geese and mallards come down on lakes, and they stay until autumn. Along the coast, herring gulls pass at any time of year.

Wary birds
Waterbirds remember being disturbed. Every time a flock is flushed, it becomes warier and flees from further away. A flock flushed or shot at again and again gives the place up: it leaves, and for about two days no waterbirds settle within some 60 blocks of it. A careful hunter gets about two geese from a flock before it goes. It is the place they learn to avoid, not the hunter, and they calm down after a day or so. Gulls are bolder and take much longer to drive off.

Crows and crops
Crows raid farmland: now and then one flies over to a crop and eats it, killing it as hares and deer do. Fences don't stop them, but a straw dummy does: crows won't raid crops or come down to feed within 15 blocks of a standing one, crows already there fly off, and they never get used to it.

Owls at night
Tawny owls keep to the trees. By day they roost hidden in the crowns; after dusk they sit out in the open at the edge of the trees, on tree tops, fence posts and walls, hooting, and drop onto the wood mice that come out in the grass. An owl that has eaten doesn't hunt again for a while.

Hunting
Birds are quick: arrows and other shot bring them down, but they dodge spears and blows and fly off. A sneaking hunter gets closer before they notice. They give poultry and plenty of feathers.

The birds
Greylag goose, mallard, grey heron, golden eagle, herring gull, carrion crow and tawny owl. Common cranes only ever pass over.
